name: Japanese
notes: Start with hiragana — it is a true alphabet of 46 sounds and can be learned in a week. Once you can read it, everything else in Japanese becomes approachable. Japanese has no tones and very regular pronunciation, which makes speaking it far easier than reading it.
syllabus: These decks cover both kana in full (JLPT N5 needs both), about 40 of the 100 N5 kanji, and under a tenth of the 800 or so N5 words. N5 is the first of five official levels; passing it means simple, slow conversations. The decks are a survival core to build on, not a course — the guide says what to add next.
